imageCaption: Operation Frequent Wind, April 29-30, 1975. US Marine helicopters conducted 81 sorties evacuating approximately 7,000 people from Saigon as North Vietnamese forces entered the city.

longForm.title: The Fall of Saigon, April 1975: What the Last Helicopter Carried
longForm.excerpt: On April 29, 1975, Armed Forces Radio played 'White Christmas' over Saigon at 6:15 in the morning. The crowd outside the Embassy gates understood what the song meant. The question was whether they would be on the right side of the gates when the helicopters stopped.
paragraphs: April 29, 1975. Saigon. At 6:15 in the morning, Armed Forces Radio plays 'White Christmas.' It is not Christmas. The song is the pre-arranged signal that Operation Frequent Wind — the helicopter evacuation of the American mission and its Vietnamese dependents — has begun. Outside the US Embassy on Thong Nhat Boulevard, a crowd has been forming since before dawn. They know what the song means. They have known for days that the end was coming. What they do not know is whether they will be on the right side of the gates when the helicopters stop.

The collapse that produced April 29 had been running for six weeks. The North Vietnamese Army's Ho Chi Minh Campaign began in early April 1975, following the fall of Hue on March 25 and Da Nang on March 29. The ARVN, without American air support, without the logistical backing that had sustained it for a decade, had been fragmented rather than defeated — it had simply ceased to function as a coherent force in the face of the NVA's final offensive. President Nguyen Van Thieu resigned on April 21 and fled to Taiwan, delivering a speech that blamed the United States. Ambassador Graham Martin, who had been telling Washington that the situation was manageable and that Saigon would hold, continued communicating optimism to Washington into the last week of April. The optimism was not the product of the intelligence available. Martin had commitments he was not ready to abandon, relationships he was not ready to end. On the morning of April 29, when NVA rockets hit Tan Son Nhut air base and killed the last two Americans to die in the war — Marine Lance Corporals Darwin Judge and Charles McMahon — the fiction that the city would hold could not be maintained.

Operation Frequent Wind ran for eighteen hours, from the morning of April 29 through 07:53 on the morning of April 30. US Marine CH-46 Sea Knight and CH-53 Sea Stallion helicopters flew continuous sorties between the fleet offshore and the two primary evacuation points: the Embassy compound on Thong Nhat and the CIA-operated building at 22 Gia Long Street. The crowd outside the Embassy gates was not static. It grew throughout the day. Some of those in the crowd had worked for the Americans — translators, drivers, intelligence assets, people whose presence on a North Vietnamese list was not hypothetical. Others had simply run out of other options. The Embassy's Marine Security Guard detachment, reduced as the day wore on, held the perimeter. The helicopters kept coming. By nightfall on April 29, approximately 6,000 people had been evacuated. Several thousand more remained in the city who would not get out.

The photograph that defined the fall of Saigon was taken from a rooftop by UPI photographer Hubert van Es at approximately 2:30 in the afternoon on April 29. It shows an Air America helicopter on the roof of 22 Gia Long Street, a CIA facility, with a line of people climbing a ladder to board it. The image was reproduced across the American press and became the visual emblem of the American exit from Vietnam. It is almost always described as showing people evacuating from the Embassy rooftop. It does not. The Embassy is elsewhere. The distinction matters only because the image is frequently cited as the clearest picture of what the American departure looked like — and what it actually shows is a single building, a single helicopter, a single moment of extraction in a city-wide operation that involved 81 helicopter sorties and approximately 7,000 evacuees. The image is accurate as far as it goes. It goes less far than it appears.

Martin waited until the last possible moment to leave. He had spent the day in the Embassy, overseeing the evacuation, unwilling to give the order that would end American presence in Saigon definitively. At approximately 04:58 on the morning of April 30, following a direct order from President Ford relayed through Secretary of State Kissinger, Martin boarded a helicopter from the Embassy rooftop. He carried the folded American flag from the Embassy's flagpole. The last Marine Security Guard detachment — eleven men — was lifted out at 07:53. The crowd was still outside the gates when the last helicopter lifted. The gates were locked. Some of the people outside the gates had been there since before dawn the previous day.

At 10:45 in the morning of April 30, 1975, NVA Tank 843 of the 203rd Armored Brigade crashed through the gates of the Independence Palace — the Reunification Palace. A crew member climbed out and planted a North Vietnamese flag on the facade. Colonel Bui Tin, who had entered the palace as part of the advance, received the formal surrender from General Duong Van Minh, who had been president of South Vietnam for forty-three hours. Bui Tin's response to Minh's offer of surrender has been quoted in subsequent accounts: 'There is no question of your surrendering. Only the Communists have won.' Whether Bui Tin said exactly those words in that sequence has been disputed; his own account has varied. What is not disputed is that at 11:30 in the morning, the flag of the People's Army of Vietnam was raised over the building, and the Republic of South Vietnam ceased to exist.

The people who had been outside the Embassy gates when the last helicopter lifted were not evacuated. Some made their way to the port and boarded vessels that joined the flotilla of South Vietnamese Navy ships and refugee boats moving toward the fleet offshore. Approximately 130,000 South Vietnamese refugees were evacuated in the days and weeks following April 30. Many more were not. The ones who had worked most closely with the Americans — intelligence assets, police officials, military officers above a certain rank — faced a particular reckoning. The North Vietnamese government announced re-education camps as the mechanism for processing former South Vietnamese military and government personnel. The camps held people for periods ranging from months to more than a decade. The definition of who required re-education expanded as the occupation consolidated.

Twenty years of American involvement in Vietnam ended with a helicopter lifting from a rooftop in the dark before dawn. The strategic assessment of that involvement has been argued since. What the record of April 29-30, 1975, shows most clearly is not the strategic failure — that had been coming since at least 1968 — but the specific gap between the commitments made and the commitments kept. The people outside the Embassy gates had made calculations based on those commitments. The helicopters that did not come back had their reasons. Those reasons did not change what happened to the people left outside the gates.

shortForm.title: Ambassador Graham Martin and the Last Stand of American Credibility in Saigon
shortForm.excerpt: Graham Martin was the last American ambassador to South Vietnam. He spent the final weeks of April 1975 acting on a belief the evidence no longer supported. The record of what that cost is not in the strategic assessment. It is in the list of people who were outside the Embassy gates when the helicopters stopped.
paragraphs: Graham Martin arrived in Saigon as US Ambassador in July 1973, eighteen months after the Paris Peace Accords, into a mission that everyone who was paying attention understood was managing a terminal situation. Martin did not manage it that way. He believed, or chose to act as if he believed, that South Vietnam could survive with American material support and without American combat forces — that the Thieu government was viable, that the ARVN could hold, that the political will in Washington to sustain the commitment would not collapse. All three premises were wrong, and the evidence for their being wrong accumulated through 1974 and into 1975. Martin filtered that evidence through his commitment to the mission. Washington filtered it through a Congress that had cut off funding for military operations in Southeast Asia and a public that had no appetite for re-engagement.

Martin's behavior in the final weeks of April 1975 was the product of a particular kind of institutional loyalty: a refusal to act on the information that the cause was lost until the loss was physically unavoidable. He delayed ordering the evacuation of American non-essential personnel because ordering that evacuation would signal to the South Vietnamese government and military that the Americans were leaving — and he believed that signal would accelerate the collapse he was trying to prevent. He was probably right that the signal would accelerate the collapse. He was wrong to believe that delaying the signal would prevent it. The collapse happened anyway. The delay in ordering full evacuation shortened the time available to get Vietnamese allies out.

On the morning of April 30, Martin carried the Embassy flag off the rooftop. It was the gesture of a man who understood that something real was ending, even if he had spent weeks refusing to act on that understanding. The critique of Martin's conduct is not that he was dishonest or cowardly. It is that he allowed a personal commitment to a policy position to override his professional obligation to protect the people in his care — both the American personnel under his authority and the Vietnamese allies whose safety depended on early action. The record of April 29 is, among other things, the record of what happens when a diplomat cannot separate what he believes from what the evidence shows.

onThisDay.headline: U-Boats Attack Convoy ONS 5 in the North Atlantic
onThisDay.body: On May 4, 1943, German U-boats mounted sustained attacks against Allied convoy ONS 5 in the North Atlantic, sinking several merchant ships in one of the final major convoy battles before catastrophic losses forced the Kriegsmarine to withdraw from the Atlantic. May 1943 — later called Black May — cost Germany 41 submarines, ending the U-boat threat as a strategic force.
